 This means owning the full loop: defining what the agent should be able to do (through user story mapping and validation with real engineers), building and benchmarking the agent against those stories, setting and enforcing token budgets per problem, and expanding the agent's coverage until it handles the workflows that matter most to customers. You'll be measured on agent task success rate, token efficiency, and workflow coverage — not on how clever the architecture is.
   

  

**What You'll Do**
**Agent Performance \& Evaluation**
* Drive agent task success rate. Own the metric that matters most — can the agent actually complete the workflows engineers need? Define the eval framework, establish baselines, and systematically improve performance.
* Set and enforce token budgets per problem. Every workflow has a cost. You'll define per\-task token budgets, track cost per completed workflow, and make the agent efficient enough to be commercially viable — not just technically impressive.
* Build the evaluation infrastructure. Design benchmarks grounded in real user stories, not synthetic tasks. Think SWE\-bench\-level rigor applied to engineering workflows — reproducible, adversarial, and tied to actual customer value.


**User Story Mapping \& Workflow Coverage**
* Lead user story mapping and validation. Work directly with the user researcher and domain expert contractors to interview engineers, document their workflows in detail, and validate that the stories you're building against reflect reality — not assumptions.
* Expand workflow coverage. Systematically increase the percentage of steps in top user stories that the agent can handle end\-to\-end. You'll prioritize which workflows to tackle based on customer value and technical feasibility.
* Translate user stories into evals. Every validated user story becomes a test case. You'll close the loop between user research and agent benchmarking.


**Technical Leadership**
* Own the agent architecture. Tool\-calling strategies, state management across multi\-step workflows, error recovery, model routing, context management — you'll make the foundational technical decisions and own their consequences.
* Lead a team of AI engineers. Set technical direction, review architecture decisions, unblock the team, and raise the engineering bar. You're a player\-coach — you'll write code and you'll lead others.
* Collaborate cross\-functionally. Work with the integration team to define what capabilities the agent needs from each tool, with the product team on how the agent surfaces to users, and with customers during POCs to close the feedback loop between agent behavior and real\-world usage.


**What We're Looking For**
* 7\+ years in software engineering, with at least 2 years building agentic AI systems — LLM\-based agents that take actions in the real world, not just generate text. You've built agents that call tools, manage state across multi\-step tasks, handle failures, and operate under cost constraints.
* Deep experience with LLM application architecture. Prompt engineering is table stakes. You've made hard decisions about model selection, context window management, retrieval strategies, tool\-calling frameworks, and orchestration patterns. You understand the tradeoffs between agent autonomy and reliability.
* Strong evaluation and benchmarking instincts. You've built eval frameworks for agentic systems — not just accuracy metrics, but task completion, cost efficiency, failure mode analysis, and regression detection. Familiarity with benchmarks like SWE\-bench, GAIA, τ\-bench, or similar is a strong signal.
* Experience leading a small technical team. You've set technical direction for 3–6 engineers, done meaningful code review, and made architecture decisions that the team executed against. Formal management experience is not required — technical leadership is.
* Strong in Python, with working knowledge of the LLM tooling ecosystem (function calling, tool use APIs, tracing/observability tools like Logfire or LangSmith, evaluation frameworks).
* Bias toward measurement and shipping. You'd rather ship an agent that completes 70% of a workflow reliably than an elegant system that demos well but can't be measured.


**Nice to Have**
* Experience with desktop automation, COM, or controlling applications programmatically (not just web APIs).
* Background in mechanical engineering, CAD/CAE, PLM, or adjacent industries.
* Experience building or contributing to public benchmarks for AI agents.
* Familiarity with enterprise deployment constraints — how the agent behaves when it's running on a locked\-down corporate workstation, not a clean dev environment.
* Published work or open\-source contributions in agentic AI systems.


**Why This Role**
* This is the core problem. Everything else at Cosmon exists to support the agent. You own the thing that makes the product valuable.
* Real\-world agentic AI, not a research project. The agent controls real desktop software in real enterprise environments for real customers. The feedback loop is tight and the stakes are high.
* Build the eval framework for a new domain. Engineering workflow automation has no established benchmark. You'll define what good looks like — for Cosmon and potentially for the field.
* Early\-stage leverage. Small team, Series A, Fortune 100 customers, direct line to the CTO. Your technical decisions become the company's technical direction.
